subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: In the PEACE approach immediately after an acute soft-tissue injury, the letter P refers to:
options: Performance testing in this case
Passive stretching in this case
Progressive running in this case
Protection of the injured area
explanation: PEACE begins with protection of the injured area from aggravating load; it is not a prescription for complete immobilisation.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: In the PEACE approach, E stands for:
options: Electrical stimulation in this case
Eccentric exercise in this case
Elevation of the injured area
Emergency referral in this case
explanation: Elevation is used as part of early care to help limit swelling; the acronym is not a treatment sequence for exercise selection.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: The A in PEACE refers to avoiding routine use of:
options: All active movement for this athlete
Athletic taping in the acute phase
Avoid routine anti-inflammatory use
Assessment of pain for this athlete
explanation: The PEACE framework cautions against routine anti-inflammatory strategies when they may interfere with aspects of tissue healing; clinical context still matters.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: The C in PEACE stands for:
options: Compression of the injured area
Cryotherapy only in this case
Cardiorespiratory training
Closed-chain exercise in this case
explanation: Compression is included in the early management acronym to help manage swelling and provide support.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: The E in PEACE refers to:
options: Electrical muscle testing in this case
Education about recovery and loading
End-range mobilisation in this case
Emergency medication for this athlete
explanation: Education helps the athlete understand the injury, prognosis and active recovery plan.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: In the LOVE framework, optimal loading is introduced primarily to:
options: Guarantee pain-free training immediately
Stimulate tissue adaptation and function
Prevent all inflammatory activity in this case
Replace clinical reassessment in this case
explanation: Progressive, tolerable loading supports recovery and function; it must be adjusted to symptoms and tissue response.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: A footballer has a stable ankle sprain 48 hours after injury. Which plan best reflects optimal loading?
options: Complete bed rest until swelling disappears during early management
Repeated maximal sprinting to test stability in the acute phase
Aggressive stretching into sharp pain before progressive loading
Protected weight bearing with gradual, symptom-guided progression
explanation: Stable injuries generally benefit from protected movement and progressive loading rather than prolonged rest or provocative testing.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: The main limitation of using the old RICE acronym as a complete rehabilitation plan is that it:
options: Requires a radiograph for every sprain
Does not describe progressive loading
Prohibits compression in acute care
Defines return to sport precisely
explanation: RICE may describe early symptom management but does not provide a complete criteria-based recovery pathway.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: After a calf strain, pain rises during a prescribed exercise and remains markedly worse the next morning. The best adjustment is to:
options: Reduce or modify the load and reassess response
Double the volume to accelerate adaptation
Stop all movement for several weeks in this case
Ignore the delayed symptom response in this case
explanation: The next-day response is useful load-monitoring information; a disproportionate flare suggests that the current dose needs modification.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: For an uncomplicated acute soft-tissue injury, early movement should generally be:
options: Within tolerable symptoms and limits
Forced through severe pain in this case
Avoided until all bruising resolves
Performed only with maximal resistance
explanation: Early movement is individualized and should respect tissue irritability, pain and functional safety.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: An athlete with a suspected fracture after a collision should receive which priority before a loading programme?
options: Immediate eccentric strengthening for this athlete
Deep massage over the injury in the acute phase
Maximal range-of-motion testing during assessment
Immobilisation and appropriate medical assessment
explanation: Possible fracture changes the pathway: protect the area and obtain appropriate assessment before therapeutic loading.

text: Body mass index is calculated as:
options: Body mass in kilograms divided by height in metres
Height in metres divided by body mass in kilograms
Body mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
Body-fat percentage multiplied by body mass
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, defines BMI as body mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

subtopic: Acute soft-tissue protocols and optimal loading
text: Why is optimal loading preferable to a universal rest prescription after many soft-tissue injuries?
options: It eliminates the need for diagnosis during early management
Matches load to tissue capacity while maintaining function
It guarantees identical recovery times in the acute phase
It permits maximal loading from day one in the acute phase
explanation: Loading can preserve function and stimulate adaptation, but it must be individualized, monitored and progressed rather than maximal from the outset.

text: Hamstring strain injuries most commonly occur during:
options: Low-load walking only during return-to-running
Relaxed breathing exercises in this athlete
High-speed running or forceful lengthening
Static sitting without movement in a sprinter
explanation: Hamstrings are challenged at high speed and long muscle lengths, particularly during late swing and terminal stance demands.

text: The hamstring group contributes primarily to:
options: Hip abduction and knee extension
Hip extension and knee flexion
Ankle inversion and hip flexion
Knee rotation and elbow flexion
explanation: The hamstrings cross both hip and knee, extending the hip and flexing the knee.

text: A typical clinical feature that should be documented after a hamstring injury is:
options: Only resting heart rate in a sprinter
Visual acuity alone in this athlete
Pain location and resisted loading
Hand grip symmetry in this athlete
explanation: Location, palpation, range and resisted loading help characterize the injury and guide progression.

text: During early rehabilitation of a painful hamstring strain, the most appropriate loading emphasis is usually:
options: Maximal sprinting during hamstring rehabilitation
Aggressive ballistic stretching during return-to-running
Low-irritability isometric or controlled strengthening
Complete unloading for the entire season in a sprinter
explanation: Early controlled loading can maintain capacity while limiting excessive irritability; intensity progresses with symptoms and function.

text: The biceps femoris long head is clinically important because it is:
options: The only muscle crossing the hip in a sprinter
A rotator-cuff muscle during return-to-running
A frequently injured hamstring in sprinting
A primary ankle dorsiflexor in this athlete
explanation: The biceps femoris long head is frequently involved in high-speed running-related hamstring injuries.

text: Before progressing a hamstring rehabilitation programme to high-speed running, the clinician should first establish:
options: A completely normal resting ECG in every athlete
Tolerance of progressive strength and running loads
Pain-free maximal stretching only during assessment
A fixed calendar date for return in this athlete
explanation: High-speed exposure should follow demonstrated capacity under progressively more demanding strength and running tasks.

text: A useful principle when reintroducing sprinting after hamstring injury is to:
options: Begin with repeated maximal sprints
Use speed only after full competitive return
Avoid all running until strength is perfect
Progress running speed and volume
explanation: Running exposure is graded from lower to higher demand and is monitored for symptoms and next-day response.

text: An athlete reports no pain during jogging but pain during maximal sprinting. The next step should be to:
options: Declare full clearance immediately in this athlete
Maintain submaximal running and gradually build speed
Stop all lower-limb exercise indefinitely in a sprinter
Test sprinting repeatedly until pain fades in a sprinter
explanation: The athlete has not yet demonstrated tolerance of the highest-speed demand; speed should be progressed in a controlled manner.

text: Which finding is more useful than time alone when judging hamstring return to sport?
options: Symmetrical strength and sport-specific running tolerance
The number of days since injury only during return-to-running
Absence of bruising alone during hamstring rehabilitation
The athlete's preference without testing in this athlete
explanation: Criteria-based progression considers strength, symptoms, running exposure and sport demands rather than time alone.

text: The Nordic hamstring exercise is primarily used to develop:
options: Passive ankle mobility
Concentric shoulder power
Respiratory muscle endurance
Eccentric hamstring strength
explanation: Nordic hamstring exercise provides a high eccentric load to the hamstrings and is used in prevention and rehabilitation programmes.

text: A late-stage hamstring programme should include exposure to:
options: High-speed running and long-length hamstring loading
Only unloaded range of motion during return-to-running
Only upper-limb resistance before high-speed running
Bed rest after every session as the initial response
explanation: The athlete must regain tolerance to the mechanisms and loads that commonly challenge the hamstrings in sport.

text: An athlete weighs 81 kg and is 1.80 m tall. The approximate BMI is:
options: 22.5 kg/m²
25.0 kg/m²
27.8 kg/m²
31.2 kg/m²
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports the BMI calculation: 81 ÷ 1.80² is approximately 25.0 kg/m².

text: Why should hamstring rehabilitation include both local strength work and running progression?
options: Running cannot load hamstrings in a sprinter
Strength testing predicts every match action
Tissue capacity plus task-specific exposure
Local exercises replace sport demands
explanation: Local strengthening develops capacity, while running progression tests the integrated high-speed task required in many sports.

text: A key early goal after ACL reconstruction is to restore:
options: Only maximal flexion strength in this athlete
Pain-free sprinting immediately in this athlete
Unrestricted pivoting in week one
Knee extension and quadriceps activation
explanation: Early restoration of extension and quadriceps function helps reduce impairments that can compromise later rehabilitation.

text: After ACL reconstruction, rehabilitation progression should be primarily:
options: Based only on a fixed calendar
Based only on the graft label in this athlete
Delayed until the athlete feels ready
Criteria-based individual progression
explanation: The Aspetar guideline supports progression using clinical and functional criteria rather than time alone.

text: An athlete after ACL reconstruction has persistent effusion and poor quadriceps control. The most appropriate response is to:
options: Progress immediately to cutting drills during rehabilitation
Ignore effusion if pain is low after ACL reconstruction
Begin unrestricted competition after ACL reconstruction
Modify loading and address impairments before progression
explanation: Effusion and poor control indicate that the current stage may not be tolerated; progression should address these impairments.

text: A common purpose of closed-chain exercise in ACL rehabilitation is to:
options: Eliminate all knee joint loading in this athlete
Train only the upper limb before return to sport
Guarantee graft healing by itself in this athlete
Functional lower-limb strength in weight bearing
explanation: Closed-chain work can develop coordinated lower-limb strength, but exercise selection and dose remain stage-dependent.

text: The quadriceps is particularly important after ACL reconstruction because weakness may impair:
options: Knee control and functional performance
Vision and vestibular balance in this athlete
Hand dexterity only during rehabilitation
Respiratory exchange during rehabilitation
explanation: Quadriceps weakness can affect gait, landing, stair function and overall lower-limb control.

text: Before introducing repeated hopping after ACL reconstruction, the clinician should confirm:
options: A normal shoulder examination only before sport-specific testing
A fixed number of postoperative days before sport-specific testing
Pain during every landing before sport-specific testing
Adequate strength, movement control and low symptom irritability
explanation: Plyometric loading follows adequate strength, control and symptom tolerance; postoperative time is only one consideration.

text: The limb symmetry index is calculated by comparing:
options: The athlete with a population average only
Flexibility with resting pulse
Involved versus uninvolved limb
Pain score with body mass
explanation: LSI commonly expresses involved-limb performance relative to the contralateral limb, though absolute benchmarks are also important.

text: A hop-test battery after ACL reconstruction is most useful when it is interpreted together with:
options: The calendar date alone before sport-specific testing
Swelling ignored by the athlete before return to sport
A single successful hop before sport-specific testing
Strength, movement quality and psychological readiness
explanation: Hop distance alone can miss movement, strength and confidence deficits; return decisions should be multidimensional.

text: The ACL reconstruction return-to-sport decision should be made by:
options: The athlete alone without assessment in this athlete
A coach using match selection only in this athlete
A single imaging report as the initial response
Team-and-athlete decision using agreed criteria
explanation: Return is a shared clinical decision based on objective findings, sport demands and athlete readiness.

text: If an athlete demonstrates a large knee valgus during a single-leg landing, the priority is to:
options: Add maximal cutting immediately during assessment
Correct landing mechanics before advancing impact
Ignore it if distance is good during rehabilitation
Stop all rehabilitation permanently in this athlete
explanation: Poor landing control is a modifiable movement deficit that should be addressed before higher-risk tasks.

text: A graft-specific rehabilitation plan should account for:
options: Donor tissue and related impairments
Only the athlete's shoe colour
The same protocol for every graft
The competition schedule alone
explanation: Bone–patellar tendon–bone, hamstring and quadriceps tendon grafts may produce different donor-site considerations.

text: A major limitation of BMI when used with a muscular athlete is that it:
options: Cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass
Requires a skinfold caliper for every calculation
Directly measures visceral fat with high precision
Is unaffected by height or body mass
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, cautions that BMI does not distinguish fat mass from fat-free mass.

text: An athlete meets distance symmetry but reports fear of re-injury during cutting. The best next step is to:
options: Clear immediately based on symmetry in this athlete
Psychological readiness and graded cutting exposure
Exclude all sport-specific practice in this athlete
Use imaging as the sole answer during rehabilitation
explanation: Performance symmetry does not eliminate fear; graded exposure and psychological support are relevant to safe return.

text: The rotator cuff primarily contributes to:
options: Glenohumeral stability and controlled rotation
Elbow extension only before throwing practice
Wrist flexion only during shoulder rehabilitation
Ankle stability during shoulder rehabilitation
explanation: The cuff compresses and guides the humeral head while producing rotation and assisting shoulder control.

text: The supraspinatus muscle is most associated with initiating:
options: Elbow flexion in this presentation
Wrist extension in this presentation
Initial shoulder abduction
Scapular depression only
explanation: Supraspinatus assists the initial phase of abduction and contributes to glenohumeral control.

text: A swimmer has shoulder pain during repeated overhead work but no traumatic loss of strength. Initial management should emphasise:
options: Immediate maximal throwing during shoulder rehabilitation
Load modification and progressive cuff/scapular exercise
Complete immobilisation for months in an overhead athlete
Repeated painful end-range testing in an overhead athlete
explanation: Many atraumatic shoulder presentations respond to modified exposure and progressive capacity-building.

text: A full-thickness rotator-cuff tear is more concerning when accompanied by:
options: Normal strength with no symptoms in this presentation
Marked weakness and loss of active elevation
Isolated painless ankle stiffness in this presentation
Improved overhead endurance in this presentation
explanation: Loss of active elevation or substantial weakness warrants careful assessment for a significant structural lesion.

text: If an overhead athlete's pain increases as weekly throwing volume rises, the most useful first intervention is to:
options: Increase throwing to build tolerance immediately
Ignore volume because pain is local in this presentation
Reduce the provocative load and monitor response
Stop all physical activity permanently
explanation: A load-response relationship supports modifying the provoking exposure while maintaining tolerable conditioning.

text: Scapular upward rotation during elevation helps the shoulder by:
options: Locking the elbow in extension
Preventing all humeral motion in this presentation
Scapular orientation for overhead motion
Increasing ankle dorsiflexion in this presentation
explanation: Scapular motion contributes to coordinated shoulder elevation and glenoid orientation.

text: A painful arc during active elevation should be interpreted as:
options: A definitive diagnosis of a cuff tear in this presentation
One finding requiring full-examination integration
Proof that exercise is contraindicated in this presentation
Evidence of a spinal fracture in this presentation
explanation: A painful arc is not diagnostic in isolation; history, strength, range and other findings refine the clinical reasoning.

text: For many non-traumatic rotator-cuff-related presentations, exercise therapy aims to improve:
options: Only passive flexibility as the initial response
Cardiac output alone during shoulder rehabilitation
Visual reaction time only in an overhead athlete
Shoulder strength, load tolerance and confidence
explanation: Progressive exercise targets capacity and function, not merely passive range.

text: An athlete with painful weakness after a fall and inability to raise the arm should first receive:
options: Maximal resisted abduction testing in this presentation
A full throwing session before throwing practice
Prompt medical assessment for significant injury
Aggressive massage over the shoulder in this presentation
explanation: Traumatic weakness and loss of active elevation warrant assessment before an exercise-only programme.

text: The infraspinatus contributes chiefly to:
options: Internal rotation of the hip
Knee extension in this presentation
Ankle plantarflexion in this presentation
External rotation of the shoulder
explanation: Infraspinatus is a major glenohumeral external rotator and stabiliser.

text: Why should shoulder rehabilitation be linked to the athlete's sport exposure?
options: Shoulder exercises have no relation to sport
Sport demand is identical for all athletes
Pain scores alone predict workload during assessment
Capacity matched to sport volume, speed and position
explanation: A throwing, swimming or contact athlete faces different shoulder loads; rehabilitation should bridge those demands progressively.

text: Skinfold assessment primarily measures:
options: Bone mineral content at selected sites
Intramuscular glycogen concentration
Total body water without an equation
Subcutaneous fat thickness
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, describes skinfolds as measures of subcutaneous fat used in prediction equations for body composition.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: A stress injury of bone generally reflects:
options: Repetitive loading exceeding bone capacity
A single painless stretch in this presentation
Only direct infection in this presentation
An isolated skin abrasion in this presentation
explanation: Stress injuries develop along a continuum when repeated load and recovery are mismatched.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: A feature that raises concern for a bone stress injury is:
options: Focal load-related bony pain
Diffuse painless muscle fatigue
Pain only in the opposite arm
Improved pain with every impact
explanation: Focal pain that is reproduced by loading warrants careful assessment and load modification.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: A runner develops focal tibial pain that persists during walking. The safest initial management is to:
options: Stop impact loading and arrange clinical assessment
Continue sprint intervals during clinical assessment
Perform repeated hop tests in a symptomatic runner
Use painkillers to complete training in this presentation
explanation: Persistent pain with walking suggests a more significant stress injury and should not be tested with further impact.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: High-risk stress fracture sites are important because they may have:
options: Guaranteed rapid healing as the initial response
Greater risk of delayed healing or complications
No need for imaging during bone-stress recovery
Only cosmetic consequences before impact resumes
explanation: Location influences prognosis and may require more urgent imaging or specialist management.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: A sudden increase in running volume with inadequate recovery is best viewed as:
options: A modifiable training-load risk factor
A protective adaptation in this presentation
An unrelated dietary fact in this presentation
A reason to avoid all future exercise
explanation: Load spikes and inadequate recovery can contribute to bone stress and other overuse injuries.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome classically produces symptoms that:
options: Remain identical at rest from the start
Occur only after eating in this presentation
Disappear permanently after one stretch
Exercise-related symptoms easing with rest
explanation: Exercise-induced, reproducible pain and tightness relieved by rest are characteristic, though diagnosis requires appropriate assessment.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: The compartment most often discussed in chronic exertional compartment syndrome of the leg is the:
options: Anterior compartment
Posterior abdominal compartment
Medial elbow compartment
Thoracic cavity
explanation: The anterior leg compartment is commonly involved, although other compartments can be affected.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: A runner with exertional leg pain also develops foot drop during exercise. This finding should prompt:
options: More hill sprints during bone-stress recovery
Urgent assessment for neurological compromise
Routine stretching only before impact resumes
Reassurance without examination in this presentation
explanation: Exercise-induced weakness or foot drop suggests nerve and pressure effects and merits prompt evaluation.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: Unlike chronic exertional compartment syndrome, acute compartment syndrome is:
options: A harmless training response
Managed with delayed review only
Defined by painless swelling
A time-critical emergency
explanation: Acute compartment syndrome can threaten tissue viability and requires urgent medical management.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: After a suspected bone stress injury, the rehabilitation goal is to:
options: Return directly to maximal impact
Use complete rest without reassessment
Staged, symptom-guided loading
Test pain tolerance daily
explanation: Healing and capacity are rebuilt progressively, with symptoms and clinical findings guiding advancement.

subtopic: Stress injuries and exertional compartment syndrome
text: Which factor can impair bone stress injury recovery?
options: Adequate fuelling and sleep
Low energy availability
Gradual loading
Appropriate recovery
explanation: Low energy availability can impair bone health and recovery and should be addressed as part of the broader assessment.

text: For repeated skinfold measurements to be more interpretable, the assessor should:
options: Change sites at every visit to avoid adaptation
Measure immediately after heavy exercise only
Use a consistent protocol, sites and trained technique
Record the largest value without checking landmarks
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, emphasises standardised sites, technique and assessor procedures for reliable repeated measures.

text: The ligament most commonly injured in a typical lateral ankle sprain is the:
options: Anterior talofibular ligament
Posterior talofibular ligament
Calcaneofibular ligament
Deltoid ligament
explanation: The anterior talofibular ligament is the most frequently injured component of the lateral ankle ligament complex.

text: A syndesmotic ankle sprain is commonly called a:
options: Low ankle sprain
Medial ankle sprain
Inversion ankle sprain
High ankle sprain
explanation: The distal tibiofibular syndesmosis is injured in what is commonly called a high ankle sprain.

text: Compared with a simple lateral ankle sprain, a syndesmotic injury often requires:
options: Slower progression with stability assessment
Immediate return to cutting in this athlete
No weight-bearing assessment in this athlete
Only passive toe stretching in this athlete
explanation: Syndesmotic injuries may remain symptomatic longer and require assessment of the distal tibiofibular complex.

text: The talar-tilt test at the ankle primarily assesses the:
options: Anterior talofibular ligament
Calcaneofibular ligament
Deltoid ligament exclusively
Plantar plate in this athlete
explanation: The ankle talar-tilt test, particularly with inversion, primarily challenges the calcaneofibular ligament.

text: A player with ankle sprain has persistent giving way after swelling settles. Rehabilitation should include:
options: Balance training with progressive ankle strengthening
Only ice indefinitely during injury rehabilitation
Repeated unprotected inversion before return to play
Upper-limb resistance alone after clinical assessment
explanation: Neuromuscular and strength training address residual instability and reduce recurrence risk.

text: A basketball player has navicular tenderness after an inversion injury. Under the Ottawa ankle rules, the next decision concerns:
options: Plain radiographs of the ankle or foot
A concussion assessment before imaging
A hamstring strength test before imaging
A return-to-play test before imaging
explanation: The Ottawa rules help identify ankle or midfoot injuries that warrant plain radiographs; they do not replace the wider examination or return-to-play testing.

text: Pain over the proximal fifth metatarsal after an inversion injury should lead to:
options: Immediate sprinting as the initial response
Deep transverse friction massage in this athlete
Clearance based only on ankle range in this athlete
Fracture assessment and appropriate imaging
explanation: The fifth metatarsal is an important bony site in ankle trauma and should be assessed rather than assumed to be a sprain.

text: Adductor-related groin pain is usually reproduced by:
options: Resisted wrist extension in this athlete
Cervical rotation only in this athlete
Passive elbow flexion in this athlete
Adductor contraction or palpation
explanation: The Doha taxonomy defines adductor-related groin pain by pain on resisted adduction and adductor palpation.

text: Iliopsoas-related groin pain is most associated with pain on:
options: Resisted ankle eversion before return to play
Passive wrist pronation before return to play
Shoulder abduction after clinical assessment
Resisted hip flexion or iliopsoas palpation
explanation: Iliopsoas-related groin pain is assessed with relevant resisted hip-flexion and palpation findings.

text: A footballer with adductor-related groin pain should initially receive:
options: Repeated maximal kicking through pain before return to play
Complete inactivity without reassessment in this athlete
Load modification and progressive adductor strengthening
Only lumbar traction during injury rehabilitation
explanation: Progressive adductor loading and modification of provocative sport exposure are central to rehabilitation.

text: The Copenhagen adduction exercise primarily loads the:
options: Rotator cuff in this athlete
Hip adductor loading
Cervical extensors
Wrist flexors
explanation: Copenhagen variations provide substantial adductor loading and are used in groin conditioning and prevention.

text: An athlete returns to training after an ankle sprain but still cannot perform repeated single-leg hops. The appropriate decision is to:
options: Clear based on jogging alone in this athlete
Rehabilitation before unrestricted return
Test maximal cutting in competition
Ignore the hop deficit before return to play
explanation: Repeated hopping challenges ankle strength, control and impact tolerance relevant to sport.

text: Which measurement is a direct anthropometric circumference measure commonly used in body-composition interpretation?
options: Resting respiratory quotient
Waist circumference
Serum creatine kinase
Maximal oxygen uptake
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, includes circumference measures such as waist circumference within anthropometric assessment.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: Return to sport is best defined as a process involving:
options: A single clearance date for this athlete
Only absence of swelling for this athlete
Progression toward sport participation
Immediate return to competition
explanation: Return is a continuum from rehabilitation to participation and performance, not a single event.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: A commonly used limb symmetry target for hop testing is approximately:
options: 40 percent or less for this athlete
60 percent exactly for this athlete
Approximately 90 percent or greater
100 percent in every measure
explanation: Many clinical programmes use approximately 90% symmetry as one criterion, while also considering absolute performance and quality.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: An athlete reaches 92% hop symmetry but lands with poor knee control. The finding means:
options: Clearance is automatic during final assessment
Landing quality is irrelevant for this athlete
The uninvolved limb is injured for this athlete
Symmetry alone is insufficient for clearance
explanation: Distance symmetry can conceal movement-quality deficits; both should inform the decision.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: The ACL-RSI questionnaire is intended to assess:
options: Bone density in a criteria-based decision
Psychological readiness after ACL injury
Ankle range of motion for this athlete
Cardiorespiratory fitness for this athlete
explanation: ACL-RSI addresses emotions, confidence and appraisal related to returning to sport.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: An athlete meets strength criteria but reports high fear of reinjury. A useful intervention is:
options: Graded sport exposure with psychological support
Forced competition to build confidence for this athlete
Ignoring the fear during return-to-sport testing
Removing all decision-making from the athlete
explanation: Confidence can be developed through graded exposure, education and appropriate psychological support.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: A return-to-sport test battery should include tasks that reflect:
options: Only the easiest clinic exercise
Sport demands and fatigue conditions
Only resting flexibility for this athlete
An unrelated upper-body task
explanation: Testing should challenge relevant force, speed, direction, skill and fatigue demands in a controlled progression.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: If pain remains stable during training but worsens substantially the following day, the athlete should:
options: Increase volume immediately for this athlete
Assume the injury is healed for this athlete
Use the next match as the test for this athlete
Reduce recent load and reassess recovery
explanation: Delayed symptom response can indicate that the current training dose exceeds recoverable capacity.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: A return-to-play decision should be based on:
options: Time since surgery alone during final assessment
The coach's selection decision alone for this athlete
One pain score alone in a criteria-based decision
Multidimensional clinical and functional criteria
explanation: Multidimensional criteria and shared clinical decision-making are safer than a single variable.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: A goalkeeper returning after knee injury has passed linear running but not diving drills. The next step is to:
options: Progress controlled sport-specific diving
Clear because straight running is normal
Skip goalkeeper-specific practice
Begin maximal fatigue drills immediately
explanation: The athlete needs graded exposure to the specific movements and loads required in the sport.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: The term return to performance implies that the athlete has:
options: Only attended one practice for this athlete
Stopped all rehabilitation for this athlete
Capacities needed for previous performance
Recovered resting range alone for this athlete
explanation: Performance is a higher target than simply participating and may require further conditioning after medical return.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: Why can athlete preference not replace objective return-to-sport assessment?
options: Preferences are never relevant for this athlete
Objective tests predict every injury exactly
Athletes cannot participate in decisions
Motivation does not prove tissue capacity
explanation: Athlete values and goals matter, but they must be integrated with clinical evidence and risk information.

subtopic: Return to sport and psychological readiness
text: A staged return-to-sport progression commonly moves from:
options: Competition to complete rest to testing
Controlled training to competition
Maximal competition to basic mobility
Passive treatment directly to finals
explanation: A graded sequence increases sport demand stepwise and monitors the athlete's response.

text: An athlete loses 2 kg over a training block. Which conclusion is most defensible without further assessment?
options: The change may include fluid and tissue
All the loss was fat mass
All the loss was muscle mass
The change proves better performance
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports interpreting body-mass change with additional measures because mass alone cannot identify the tissues or fluid responsible.

text: A central aim of neuromuscular injury-prevention programmes is to improve:
options: Only passive joint laxity for this squad
Strength, balance and movement control
Visual acuity during athlete screening
Resting blood pressure alone for this squad
explanation: Prevention programmes target modifiable physical and movement factors associated with injury risk.

text: For a prevention programme to influence injury risk, the most important implementation factor is:
options: One session performed before a final for this squad
Random exercise selection during implementation
Regular, correct and progressive participation
Painful maximal loading every day for this squad
explanation: Adherence, technique and progression determine whether a programme is meaningfully delivered.

text: The Nordic hamstring programme is chiefly associated with reducing:
options: Wrist fracture risk
Hamstring injury risk
Concussion severity
Shoulder dislocation risk
explanation: Nordic hamstring exercise is used in prevention programmes to improve eccentric hamstring capacity.

text: The Copenhagen adduction programme targets prevention of:
options: Cervical sprain for this squad
Rotator-cuff tear for this squad
Groin and adductor problems
Heat illness for this squad
explanation: Copenhagen adduction exercises strengthen the adductor group and are used in groin-injury prevention.

text: An injury-screening test should be used primarily to:
options: Inform risk discussion and targeted intervention
Guarantee who will be injured before the season
Replace clinical history as the initial response
Exclude every athlete with asymmetry for this squad
explanation: Screening findings are not deterministic diagnoses; they help guide monitoring and preventive action.

text: The Functional Movement Screen is best interpreted as:
options: A movement screen requiring context
A definitive injury diagnosis
A measure of aerobic threshold
A replacement for sport skill testing
explanation: A screen identifies movement observations; it should not be treated as a stand-alone diagnostic or prediction tool.

text: A team screening programme finds poor landing control in several athletes. The best response is to:
options: Targeted neuromuscular training and reassessment
Label them as injured without examination
Remove them from all sport during implementation
Ignore the pattern in a team prevention plan
explanation: Screening should lead to an appropriate intervention and monitoring plan rather than automatic diagnosis.

text: A pre-participation examination commonly includes:
options: History, risk assessment and physical examination
Only a flexibility photograph before the season
Only a maximal sprint in a team prevention plan
Only a coach interview in a team prevention plan
explanation: PPE is used to identify health risks and guide safe participation and follow-up.

text: The Beighton score is used to screen for:
options: Generalised joint hypermobility
Heat acclimatisation for this squad
Hamstring strength for this squad
Concussion recovery for this squad
explanation: The Beighton score is a screening measure for selected features of generalized joint hypermobility.

text: An athlete with marked joint hypermobility and recurrent sprains should receive:
options: Automatic exclusion from sport for this squad
Only passive stretching during implementation
Repeated end-range loading during assessment
Individualised strength and control planning
explanation: Hypermobility may require improved strength and control with tailored management rather than blanket exclusion.

text: Why should injury-prevention programmes be adapted to a team's context?
options: All teams have identical risks for this squad
A single programme eliminates all injuries
Context shapes prevention implementation
Context has no effect on adherence
explanation: Effective prevention considers the sport, schedule, population, coaching environment and practical adherence.

text: A dehydrated athlete shows a lower body mass before testing. The body-composition result should be interpreted with caution because:
options: The mass change proves fat loss
Dehydration raises lean tissue quickly
Body mass is unrelated to fluid balance
Hydration can alter mass and estimates
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports standardised testing and cautions that hydration status affects body-mass interpretation and some methods.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: The primary survey is used to identify:
options: Long-term strength deficits
Immediate life threats
Detailed return-to-play criteria
Minor flexibility asymmetries
explanation: The primary survey prioritises conditions that threaten life or immediate physiological stability.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: In a collapsed athlete, the first priority is to assess:
options: Hamstring flexibility at a sports venue
Responsiveness and normal breathing
Ankle range as the initial response
Training history at a sports venue
explanation: Initial responsiveness and breathing checks determine the need for immediate resuscitation steps.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: An unresponsive athlete is not breathing normally. The team should:
options: Activate emergency response, CPR and AED access
Wait for a physician without acting at a sports venue
Give oral fluids during the initial response
Move the athlete for a stretching test
explanation: Early activation, CPR and prompt AED use are central to the chain of survival.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: The C in a <C>ABCDE primary survey represents:
options: Cervical stretching
Cardiac rehabilitation
Calf assessment
Catastrophic haemorrhage
explanation: Catastrophic external bleeding is addressed before the remaining primary-survey sequence.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: During airway management after trauma, the clinician should also consider:
options: Immediate neck rotation
Forced sitting at a sports venue
Cervical-spine protection
Unrestricted flexion
explanation: Airway care after trauma must account for possible cervical injury and use appropriate stabilisation.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: A conscious athlete with severe external bleeding should first receive:
options: Repeated active stretching at a sports venue
Oral analgesia only during on-field care
Ice placed over clothing without pressure
Direct pressure and haemorrhage control
explanation: Direct pressure and emergency escalation are appropriate initial measures for major external bleeding.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: An AED is designed to:
options: Measure blood glucose only at a sports venue
Replace chest compressions at a sports venue
Analyse rhythm and shock when indicated
Diagnose ligament injury at a sports venue
explanation: The AED guides the rescuer and shocks shockable rhythms; CPR continues as instructed.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: An athlete with suspected spinal trauma should be moved:
options: By pulling the arms quickly during on-field care
Move only when necessary with spinal precautions
After unrestricted neck testing at a sports venue
Only after asking the athlete to stand at a sports venue
explanation: Unnecessary movement can worsen injury; movement is coordinated with stabilisation and emergency priorities.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: The secondary survey is performed:
options: After immediate life threats are addressed
Before checking breathing at a sports venue
Instead of resuscitation during assessment
Only after return to sport at a sports venue
explanation: A focused history and head-to-toe assessment follow primary stabilisation and do not delay life-saving care.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: An EAP rehearsal is valuable because it:
options: Identifies operational problems before an emergency
Guarantees no emergency will occur at a sports venue
Replaces first-aid training as the initial response
Eliminates the need for equipment during assessment
explanation: Rehearsal tests communication, access, equipment and role clarity in the actual venue.

subtopic: Emergency action plans and primary survey
text: Why should emergency care be practiced by the whole sports team rather than one clinician?
options: Emergency care requires coordinated team actions
Only one person can use an AED during assessment
Team members cannot share roles at a sports venue
Practice has no effect on response at a sports venue
explanation: A coordinated response is more robust when multiple trained people know their roles and can support the primary responder.

text: A small change in a skinfold measurement that is within the method’s expected measurement error should be:
options: Treat it as definite fat loss
Convert it directly to performance gain
Interpret it cautiously as possible change
Use it to diagnose endocrine disease
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, supports considering measurement error and standardisation before interpreting small changes in skinfold-derived estimates.

text: The SCAT6 is intended primarily for use by:
options: Untrained spectators as a clearance tool
Healthcare-professional concussion assessment
Coaches as a substitute for diagnosis in this athlete
Athletes to self-clear immediately in this athlete
explanation: SCAT6 supports healthcare-professional assessment and is not a stand-alone return-to-play clearance instrument.

text: Which symptom is a concussion red flag requiring urgent referral?
options: Deteriorating consciousness
Mild thirst after exercise
Stable pre-existing freckles
Transient shoe discomfort
explanation: Deteriorating consciousness is a serious red flag and requires urgent emergency evaluation.

text: An athlete with suspected concussion reports neck pain and weakness in an arm. The priority is to:
options: Begin balance drills during concussion management
Allow return after a short rest after a head impact
Perform forceful neck mobilisation in this athlete
Spinal precautions and urgent emergency assessment
explanation: Neck pain and neurological symptoms raise concern for cervical or neurological injury and require urgent care.

text: The Amsterdam consensus recommends that concussion management begin with:
options: Strict dark-room rest for weeks after a head impact
Immediate maximal exercise as the initial response
Relative rest followed by symptom-limited activity
No monitoring of symptoms before return to play
explanation: The consensus supports relative rest initially and gradual symptom-limited activity rather than prolonged strict rest.

text: During early concussion recovery, mild symptom increase during activity should generally lead to:
options: Adjust activity dose to remain tolerable
Immediate full competition in this athlete
Ignoring all symptoms after a head impact
Complete bed rest for a month in this athlete
explanation: Activity is progressed within tolerable symptom limits, with dose adjusted when symptoms are excessive or prolonged.

text: Return-to-sport after concussion should be:
options: A single same-day decision in this athlete
Based on symptom concealment in this athlete
Determined only by team ranking in this athlete
Graduated stages with medical oversight
explanation: A graduated progression allows assessment of response as cognitive and physical demands increase.

text: Return-to-learn refers to a graded return to:
options: Weightlifting only in this athlete
Travel medicine in this athlete
Cognitive and study activities
Emergency surgery in this athlete
explanation: Return-to-learn addresses cognitive load and education participation before or alongside sport progression.

text: An athlete becomes symptom-free at rest but develops symptoms during exertion. The appropriate action is to:
options: Advance to competition in this athlete
Ignore exertional symptoms in this athlete
Stop all future exercise in this athlete
Return to the previous tolerated stage
explanation: Symptoms with exertion indicate that the current stage is not yet tolerated and progression should be adjusted.

text: A player with suspected cervical spine injury should have the neck:
options: Rotated to test range during emergency assessment
Flexed to relieve pain during emergency assessment
Manipulated before transport after a head impact
Manual stabilisation during emergency activation
explanation: Manual stabilisation and coordinated emergency care reduce unnecessary cervical movement.

text: When log-rolling a spinal-trauma patient, the safest approach is:
options: One rescuer twisting the trunk after a head impact
Coordinated movement maintaining spinal alignment
Pulling the head separately before return to play
Asking the athlete to roll alone in this athlete
explanation: A coordinated log roll preserves alignment and requires enough trained personnel for the situation.

text: The purpose of a focused concussion history includes asking about:
options: Only the athlete's shoe size during emergency assessment
Symptoms, mechanism, prior concussion and risk factors
Only current team position during emergency assessment
Only resting flexibility during concussion management
explanation: History helps identify the event, symptoms, previous injuries and factors that influence management.

text: Why should a normal brief sideline screen not be used alone to clear concussion?
options: Sideline assessment is never useful
Concussion always causes loss of consciousness
Brief screens can miss evolving deficits
Normal speech proves full recovery
explanation: A brief screen supports immediate decisions but does not replace serial assessment and a graduated return process.

text: A BMI of 27 kg/m² in an adult athlete should initially be regarded as:
options: Proof of high body fat in every athlete
A screening value that needs context
Proof of inadequate muscle mass
A direct measure of visceral fat
explanation: ACSM’s Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 12th edition, body-composition assessment chapter, uses BMI as a screening measure and notes that interpretation requires context, especially in muscular athletes.

text: The preferred immediate treatment for exertional heat stroke, when available, is:
options: Warm massage in this athlete
Oral antibiotics
Passive stretching
Cold-water immersion
explanation: Cold-water immersion rapidly removes heat and is the preferred field treatment when safely feasible.

text: A collapsed athlete in the heat is confused and hot. The team should:
options: Wait for a laboratory diagnosis in this athlete
Cold-water immersion with emergency activation
Give alcohol to promote sweating in this athlete
Send the athlete to walk it off in this athlete
explanation: Treatment and emergency activation should begin immediately; cooling should not await confirmatory testing.

text: Heat exhaustion differs from heat stroke because heat exhaustion generally lacks:
options: Sweating in every athlete
Any fatigue in this athlete
Severe CNS dysfunction
Any need for monitoring
explanation: Heat exhaustion may cause weakness, dizziness and fluid loss, but marked CNS dysfunction suggests heat stroke.

text: An athlete with suspected heat illness who is vomiting and confused should not be given:
options: Immediate cooling during field management
Large oral fluid volumes while impaired
Emergency assessment in this athlete
Removal from heat during field management
explanation: Confusion and vomiting increase aspiration risk; cooling and emergency care take priority over forced oral intake.

text: An early adaptation to heat acclimatisation is often:
options: Permanent immunity to heat illness
Reduced plasma volume in this athlete
Earlier and more effective sweating
Loss of all cardiovascular adaptation
explanation: Heat acclimatisation can improve sweating and cardiovascular strain, but it does not eliminate risk.

text: Hypothermia is characterised by:
options: Elevated temperature only during assessment
Low core temperature with impaired function
Isolated muscle hypertrophy in this athlete
Normal thermoregulation in severe exposure
explanation: Hypothermia impairs neuromuscular and physiological function and requires removal from cold and appropriate rewarming.

text: A cold, confused athlete should initially be managed by:
options: Remove wet clothing, insulate and seek care
Rubbing the skin vigorously with ice
Giving alcohol before cooling is complete
Sending the athlete back into the wind
explanation: Remove the environmental exposure, insulate and seek medical care; severe hypothermia requires careful handling.

text: Acute mountain sickness is associated with symptoms such as:
options: Headache with systemic symptoms after ascent
Only isolated ankle swelling in this athlete
Immediate tendon rupture in this athlete
Guaranteed high fever during field management
explanation: AMS commonly follows ascent and includes headache plus symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness or nausea.

text: The most important first intervention for worsening altitude illness is to:
options: Ascend faster before cooling is complete
Perform maximal intervals in this athlete
Stop ascent and arrange descent assessment
Ignore neurological symptoms in this athlete
explanation: Stopping ascent and descending when indicated are key responses to worsening altitude illness.

text: High-altitude pulmonary oedema may present with:
options: Breathlessness at rest and reduced exercise tolerance
Painless wrist stiffness before cooling is complete
Improved oxygenation with exertion in this athlete
Only local bruising during an environmental emergency
explanation: HAPE is a serious altitude emergency with respiratory symptoms, often requiring descent and urgent treatment.

text: Why should training-load monitoring include environmental stress and recovery?
options: Load is independent of climate in this athlete
Travel never affects recovery in this athlete
Environment and recovery affect illness risk
Environmental stress matters only in winter
explanation: The IOC load-and-illness framework recognises that training, environment, travel, sleep and recovery interact.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Jet lag primarily results from misalignment between the body clock and:
options: The athlete's shoe size for this squad
The local time at the destination
Muscle fibre type for this squad
The previous match score for this squad
explanation: Crossing time zones creates a mismatch between circadian timing and the new light–dark and activity schedule.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Travel fatigue can occur even without jet lag because of:
options: Only a ruptured ligament during travel planning
A required six-zone crossing during a team tour
Prolonged sitting, sleep loss and travel stress
Permanent circadian adaptation during a team tour
explanation: Travel fatigue includes factors such as disrupted sleep, prolonged sitting, dehydration and logistical stress and can precede circadian adjustment.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: For an eastward time-zone change, a practical preparation strategy is often to:
options: Advance sleep and wake times before travel
Delay sleep every night during a team tour
Use maximal exercise at local midnight
Avoid all daylight indefinitely for this squad
explanation: Eastward travel generally requires an earlier schedule; gradual pre-shifting may reduce the adjustment burden.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Light exposure is used in jet-lag management because light is a major cue for:
options: Ligament remodelling
Immediate muscle hypertrophy
Ankle proprioception
Circadian phase adjustment
explanation: Timing of light can shift the circadian clock, but recommendations should be individualized to travel direction and schedule.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: A team arriving shortly before competition should prioritise:
options: Maximal testing on arrival during a team tour
Alcohol for sleep before international travel
Sleep, hydration, light and load management
Ignoring local time as the initial response
explanation: A coordinated travel plan supports recovery and circadian adjustment while reducing unnecessary physiological stress.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: A sports medical travel kit should be based on:
options: Team risks, destination, regulations and activities
A fixed identical list for every tour for this squad
Only the coach's preferences during travel planning
Items selected after an emergency begins for this squad
explanation: Kit contents should be planned for the athletes, itinerary, destination, regulations and clinical scope.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Medication carried for an international team should be:
options: Unlabelled and shared freely for this squad
Stored without expiry checks for this squad
Documented, legal and clinically supervised
Chosen only by another athlete for this squad
explanation: Medication safety includes documentation, expiry, storage, prescription status and appropriate clinical oversight.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Before international travel, the medical team should check whether a medication is permitted under anti-doping rules because:
options: All medicines are automatically permitted
Supplements have no contamination risk
Medication may be prohibited or require a TUE
Anti-doping rules stop at the airport for this squad
explanation: Athletes have personal responsibility under anti-doping rules; medications and TUE needs should be checked in advance.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Compression garments during long travel may help reduce:
options: Concussion symptoms during a team tour
Lower-limb venous pooling and swelling
Bone stress immediately for this squad
Circadian phase delay by themselves
explanation: Compression and movement may assist circulation during prolonged sitting, but they do not replace broader travel-health measures.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: During a long flight, a practical circulation strategy is to:
options: Remain immobile throughout for this squad
Walk periodically and move the ankles
Use sedatives without advice for this squad
Avoid all fluids during a team tour
explanation: Regular movement and ankle exercises reduce prolonged immobility; hydration advice should be individualized.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: A travel medical kit should include a clear plan for:
options: Hiding medicines from the medical staff
Using expired supplies first for this squad
Removing labels from all items for this squad
Storage, access, inventory and replenishment
explanation: A usable kit requires documented inventory, secure access, storage and timely replacement.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: A team member develops diarrhoea during an overseas tour. The first management priority is to:
options: Share medication with teammates during travel planning
Continue maximal training before international travel
Assess severity, hydration and infection-control needs
Ignore red flags until return during long-haul travel
explanation: Severity, hydration, red flags and prevention of spread guide the response; persistent or severe illness needs medical assessment.

subtopic: Team travel, jet lag and medical kits
text: Why should travel plans integrate performance, medical and logistical information?
options: Travel affects only accommodation during a team tour
Travel plans integrate medical and performance needs
Medical kits solve all travel risks during a team tour
Performance is independent of sleep during a team tour
explanation: Integrated planning reduces avoidable stress and allows the team to adapt training and care to the destination.
